prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The topological structure of the event horizon has been investigated in terms of the Morse theory. The elementary process of topological evolution can be understood as a handle attachment. It has been found that there are certain constraints on the nature of black hole topological evolution: (i) There are n kinds of handle attachments in (n+1)-dimensional black hole space-times. (ii) Handles are further classified as either of black or white type, and only black handles appear in real black hole space-times. (iii) The spatial section of an exterior of the black hole region is always connected. As a corollary, it is shown that the formation of a black hole with an S**(n-2) x S**1 horizon from that with an S**(n-1) horizon must be non-axisymmetric in asymptotically flat space-times.

The topological structure of event horizons can be analyzed effectively using Morse theory. In this approach, the event horizon is regarded as a geometric object whose spatial cross-sections may change topology as one moves forward in time. Morse theory provides a systematic way to describe such changes by studying critical points of a suitable time function defined on the horizon. At ordinary points, the topology of a spatial slice remains unchanged, while at critical points the topology changes in a controlled and classifiable manner.

The elementary process underlying such a topological change is a handle attachment. A handle attachment is a standard operation in differential topology in which a piece with the form of a disk product is attached to an existing manifold, thereby modifying its topology. In the context of black hole event horizons, each critical point of the time function corresponds to the attachment of a handle. Thus, complicated changes in the topology of the horizon can be decomposed into a sequence of elementary handle-attachment processes.

For an \((n+1)\)-dimensional black hole spacetime, the event horizon is an \(n\)-dimensional hypersurface, and its spatial cross-sections are \((n-1)\)-dimensional manifolds. In this setting, there are \(n\) possible kinds of handle attachments, distinguished by their index. These different indices correspond to different ways in which the topology of the horizon cross-section can change. For example, one type of handle may create a new connected component, another may merge components, and others may create or remove higher-dimensional holes or cycles.

Handles can be classified into two types, often called black handles and white handles. This distinction reflects the time orientation of the corresponding topological process. A black handle represents a topology change compatible with the future evolution of a black hole event horizon: generators enter the horizon but do not leave it. A white handle, by contrast, would correspond to the time-reversed process, analogous to behavior associated with a white hole. In physically realistic black hole spacetimes, only black handles occur, because the causal structure of an event horizon allows null generators to join the horizon toward the future but not to exit it.

An important consequence of this analysis concerns the formation of black holes with nontrivial horizon topology. In an asymptotically flat \((n+1)\)-dimensional spacetime, the formation of a black hole whose horizon cross-section has topology  
\[
S^{n-2}\times S^1
\]
from a black hole with spherical horizon topology  
\[
S^{n-1}
\]
cannot occur through an axisymmetric process. Such a transition requires the creation of a nontrivial \(S^1\) cycle in the horizon, which corresponds to a particular handle attachment. However, under the restrictions imposed by asymptotic flatness and axisymmetry, this kind of topological evolution is obstructed. Therefore, if a black hole with horizon topology \(S^{n-2}\times S^1\), such as a higher-dimensional black ring, forms from an initially spherical black hole, the process must necessarily break axisymmetry.

The paper distinguishes the handle attachments that are compatible with the causal and geometric structure of black hole spacetimes from those that are not. The allowed transitions are referred to as “black” handle attachments, because they correspond to genuine black-hole horizon evolution.

The investigation shows that real black holes permit only certain types of these black handle attachments. One important consequence is that spatial sections of the domain of outer communication, or exterior space, remain connected during the evolution. The required handle attachment would be incompatible with the allowed black-hole topology changes under axial symmetry. Therefore, if such a transition from an \(S^{n-1}\) horizon to an \(S^{n-2} \times S^1\) horizon occurs in an asymptotically flat spacetime, it must proceed through a non-axisymmetric evolution.

Overall, the text uses Morse-theoretic methods to clarify which horizon topology changes are physically realizable in higher-dimensional black hole spacetimes. The Morse code is one of the most famous communication systems in history. It uses short and long signals, called dots and dashes, to represent letters, numbers, and punctuation. Before modern phones and the internet, Morse code helped people send messages across long distances through telegraph lines, radio waves, and flashing lights.

There is something fascinating about the simplicity of Morse code. A message can be created with sound, light, or even taps. For example, the well-known distress signal “SOS” is written as three dots, three dashes, and three dots. This made it easy to recognize in emergencies, even when communication was difficult.

The importance of Morse code goes beyond technology. It represents human creativity and the desire to stay connected. There were times when it saved lives at sea, helped soldiers communicate, and allowed news to travel faster than ever before. Even today, some radio operators and enthusiasts continue to learn and use Morse code as a skill, a hobby, and a piece of communication history.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the main findings of a paper about black hole event horizon topology studied using Morse theory, including handle attachments and constraints on horizon evolution.
counterfactuals.output:
The paper’s main point is that the topology of black-hole event horizons can be understood systematically using **Morse theory**, with changes in spatial cross-sections of the horizon corresponding to the attachment of topological “handles.”

Key findings:

- **Event horizons as evolving hypersurfaces:**  
  Although an event horizon is globally defined in spacetime, one can study its apparent “shape” by slicing spacetime into spacelike hypersurfaces. The topology of the horizon’s spatial cross-section may change depending on the slicing.

- **Morse theory describes topology change:**  
  Critical points of a suitable time function on the horizon determine when topology changes occur. Each critical point has an index, and the index tells what kind of handle is attached to the horizon cross-section.

- **Handle attachments classify horizon transitions:**  
  In four-dimensional spacetime, the possible changes of a two-dimensional horizon cross-section include:
  - creation of a new spherical component,
  - merger of two spherical components,
  - formation of a toroidal or higher-genus intermediate shape via a 1-handle,
  - disappearance or simplification of handles through higher-index critical points.

- **Black-hole mergers can temporarily have non-spherical topology:**  
  During a merger, spatial slices of the event horizon may show toroidal or more complicated topology, even though the final stationary black hole must have spherical topology under standard assumptions.

- **Constraints from horizon causality and generators:**  
  The event horizon is generated by null geodesics. New generators can enter the horizon at caustics or crossover points, but generators cannot leave toward the future. This imposes strong restrictions on allowed topology changes.

- **Not every Morse-theoretic transition is physically allowed:**  
  While Morse theory gives a formal classification of possible handle attachments, the causal structure of event horizons restricts which transitions can actually occur in black-hole spacetimes.

- **Topology change depends on slicing:**  
  The same spacetime can appear to have different intermediate horizon topologies depending on how it is foliated by time slices. Thus toroidal phases are not necessarily invariant physical objects, but features of a chosen slicing.

- **Consistency with topological censorship:**  
  The results do not contradict theorems requiring late-time black-hole horizons to be spherical. Non-spherical topologies, if they occur, are transient and slice-dependent, while the final equilibrium horizon remains topologically \(S^2\) in four-dimensional asymptotically flat spacetimes.

In short, the paper shows that Morse theory provides a precise language for describing black-hole horizon topology change: horizon mergers and transient toroidal phases correspond to handle attachments, but the causal structure of event horizons severely limits the allowed evolution.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract-style paragraph on topological evolution of event horizons in higher-dimensional black hole spacetimes, mentioning black/white handles and the impossibility of axisymmetric formation of ring horizons.
counterfactuals.output: We discuss the topological evolution of event horizons in higher-dimensional asymptotically flat black hole spacetimes, emphasizing that horizon topology change is governed not by local violations of regularity on the null hypersurface, but by the appearance and disappearance of generators at caustics and crossover sets. In this setting, transient non-spherical spatial sections may be interpreted in terms of “black handles,” which attach to an initially disconnected or spherical horizon as one evolves toward the future, and time-reversed “white handles,” which pinch off under past evolution. Such handles provide a useful geometric language for describing mergers, temporary toroidal phases, and the approach to stationary horizon topologies allowed in higher dimensions, including black-ring-like sections. However, symmetry strongly constrains these processes: an exactly axisymmetric evolution cannot generically create a ring horizon, because the required handle attachment would force the crossover set to collapse into a lower-dimensional axis, producing a singular or non-generic topology-changing event incompatible with smooth axisymmetric horizon formation. Thus, while higher-dimensional gravity admits stationary horizons with nontrivial topology, such as black rings, their dynamical formation requires sufficiently non-axisymmetric collapse or merger dynamics; ring horizons cannot arise through strictly axisymmetric evolution alone.

counterfactuals.prompt: What are the constraints on black hole topological evolution in (n+1)-dimensional spacetime according to Morse theory, and what corollary follows for forming an S^(n-2) × S^1 horizon from an S^(n-1) horizon?
counterfactuals.output:
According to Morse theory, the event horizon in an \((n+1)\)-dimensional spacetime can be treated as an \(n\)-dimensional cobordism between spatial horizon cross-sections of dimension \(n-1\). A topology change occurs only at critical points of a Morse time function on the horizon.

At a critical point of Morse index \(\lambda\), the spatial horizon changes by a \(\lambda\)-handle attachment, equivalently by the surgery

\[
S^{\lambda-1}\times D^{\,n-\lambda}
\quad \longrightarrow \quad
D^{\lambda}\times S^{\,n-\lambda-1}.
\]

Thus the allowed elementary topological evolutions are constrained by the possible Morse indices \(\lambda\). Physically, because an event horizon can merge but cannot bifurcate toward the future, the time orientation further restricts which of these Morse surgeries can occur as black-hole evolutions.

In particular, attaching a \(1\)-handle to an \((n-1)\)-sphere gives

\[
S^{n-1} \;\longrightarrow\; S^{n-2}\times S^{1}.
\]

So the corollary is:

\[
\boxed{\text{A horizon with topology } S^{n-2}\times S^1 \text{ can form from an } S^{n-1}
\text{ horizon only through an index-1 Morse critical point.}}
\]

Equivalently, the formation of a black-ring-type horizon from a spherical horizon requires a \(1\)-handle attachment. This is the higher-dimensional analogue of producing a toroidal handle on an initially spherical horizon.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a concise technical summary of research investigating event horizon topology via Morse theory and handle attachment in asymptotically flat black hole spacetimes.
counterfactuals.output:
Research on event horizon topology in asymptotically flat black hole spacetimes uses Morse theory to describe how spatial cross-sections of the event horizon change during collapse and merger. The event horizon is treated as a null hypersurface generated by null geodesics; topology change occurs at caustics or crossover points where generators enter the horizon, so smooth portions alone do not change topology.

By choosing a time function on the horizon, critical points of this function classify topology-changing events. Morse theory relates each critical point of index \(k\) to the attachment of a \(k\)-handle to a horizon cross-section. In \(3+1\) dimensions, this means:
- index 0 handles create new spherical components,
- index 1 handles merge components or create transient toroidal sections,
- index 2 handles can eliminate holes,
- index 3 handles correspond to disappearance in time-reversed descriptions.

This framework shows that non-spherical horizon slices, including toroidal or higher-genus sections, can occur depending on the spacetime slicing, even though stationary asymptotically flat black holes have spherical horizon topology under standard energy and causality assumptions. The apparent contradiction is resolved because topological censorship constrains complete causal curves and late-time stationary horizons, not arbitrary intermediate spacelike slices of the event horizon.

Handle attachment also clarifies black hole coalescence: mergers are represented by index-1 critical points connecting initially separate spherical horizons into a single component. More complicated caustic structures can yield short-lived toroidal phases, but these are slicing-dependent and not invariant properties of the event horizon. Thus Morse-theoretic analyses provide a rigorous language for classifying horizon topology change, linking global causal structure, caustics of null generators, and the transient topology of black hole merger geometries.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain, in the style of a physics paper abstract, how handle attachments classify elementary processes in event horizon topology and why black ring formation from spherical horizons must be non-axisymmetric.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract.**  
We describe topology change of event-horizon cross sections in terms of Morse theory on the null horizon hypersurface. For a \((D-1)\)-dimensional event horizon foliated by spacelike \((D-2)\)-sections, changes in horizon topology occur only at critical points of the time function restricted to the horizon, equivalently at caustics or crease-set points where new null generators enter the horizon. Each isolated critical point is classified by a Morse index \(\lambda\), and the corresponding elementary transition is the attachment of a \(\lambda\)-handle,
\[
D^\lambda \times D^{D-2-\lambda},
\]
to the spatial horizon section. Thus births, mergers, tunnel formation, and tunnel destruction are not independent phenomena but members of a single handle-attachment classification.

In five-dimensional gravity, a spherical black-hole horizon has section \(S^3\), whereas a black ring has section \(S^1\times S^2\). The transition
\[
S^3 \longrightarrow S^1\times S^2
\]
is precisely a one-handle attachment: two three-ball neighborhoods on the spherical horizon are removed and connected by a tube, producing a nontrivial \(S^1\) cycle. Hence black-ring formation from an initially spherical horizon is an elementary index-one topology-changing process.

However, this process is necessarily non-axisymmetric if it is to occur generically. In an exactly axisymmetric evolution the two localized attachment regions required for a one-handle are replaced by an entire symmetry orbit of simultaneous attachments. The critical set is then not an isolated Morse critical point but a degenerate caustic/crease set. Physically, the would-be hole of the ring closes everywhere around the symmetry axis at the same instant: null generators focus and enter the horizon coherently, preventing a finite interval in which a regular \(S^1\times S^2\) cross section is produced from a smooth spherical one. A genuine black-ring-forming handle therefore requires a localized, Morse-generic crease structure, which breaks axisymmetry. Thus, within the handle-attachment classification of event-horizon topology change, the formation of a black ring from spherical horizons is an index-one process, and its realization demands non-axisymmetric dynamics.
